passage: I'm Amandeep. When Mum's new friend Jatin came for tea the first time, he brought a box of my favourite jalebis and asked about my robot kit. I said "fine" to everything and went to my room. I was afraid that if I smiled, it would mean Dad could be replaced. Jatin never pushed. The next Sunday he just said hello and asked nothing. I stayed polite, thanked him for the jalebis, and told Mum honestly, "I'm not ready to like him." She hugged me and said that was okay. I am still slow about it, but the knot in my stomach is a little looser now.

qa.q: What did Jatin bring on his first visit?
qa.a: He brought a box of jalebis.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep say "fine" to everything and go to the bedroom?
qa.a: Amandeep was afraid that smiling would mean Dad could be replaced, so Amandeep kept a distance.

qa.q: What did Amandeep do that stayed honest without being rude?
qa.a: Amandeep stayed polite, thanked Jatin, and told Mum truthfully, "I'm not ready to like him."

qa.q: How might Jatin feel when Amandeep goes off to the bedroom?
qa.a: Jatin may feel unsure or a little rejected, but he did not push and simply said hello the next Sunday, which gives Amandeep room.

grounding: A child refuses a mother's new partner out of fear of replacement, stays polite and lets trust come slowly.

passage: I live next door and the walls are thin, so I heard all of it. Samir yelled, "That's MY sketchbook! You scribbled on my dragon page!" His younger brother Francis stood there holding a red crayon, lip trembling. Samir's face was red and his fists were tight, but he did not hit him. He snatched the sketchbook and stomped off. Later, through the balcony, I heard him say, "Next time ask me first. Mummy, can we make a rule about this?" Their mother agreed. Samir put the sketchbook on the high shelf. I can't be sure how he felt inside, but he sounded upset more than mean.

qa.q: What was Francis holding when Samir yelled?
qa.a: He was holding a red crayon.

qa.q: What do Samir's red face and tight fists suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: They suggest he was very angry, but the neighbour thinks he sounded more upset than mean, since he did not hit Francis.

qa.q: What did Samir do afterwards that worked better than hitting?
qa.a: He asked Francis to ask first, asked Mummy for a rule, and put the sketchbook on the high shelf.

qa.q: How might Francis have felt when Samir shouted?
qa.a: Francis was probably scared and sorry, since his lip trembled as he stood holding the crayon.

grounding: A neighbour observes an older brother's fair anger over a sketchbook, handled with words and a rule.

passage: I'm Tanvir. Whenever my little brother reached for my model cars, Mummy said, "Share, he is younger." Every single time. I went quiet, my anger a hard little ball. When Damini Masi visited, she noticed my scowl. "Fair is not always the same as equal," she said. I told her the plain cars were fine to share but the painted ones were mine. She said I should tell Mummy exactly that. So I did: "These three I can share. These I can't." Mummy paused. "That's reasonable," she said. I still get annoyed sometimes, but now I say it out loud instead of going silent. 🙂

qa.q: What did Mummy say whenever Tanvir's brother reached for the cars?
qa.a: She said, "Share, he is younger."

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling when going quiet each time the order to share came?
qa.a: Tanvir felt the rule was unfair and kept the anger inside like a hard little ball.

qa.q: What did Tanvir do to make the sharing fairer?
qa.a: Tanvir told Mummy exactly which cars could be shared and which were not, and she agreed it was reasonable.

qa.q: How might Mummy have seen Tanvir's silence before the explanation?
qa.a: She may have thought Tanvir was fine with sharing, since Tanvir said nothing; the explanation helped her see what was fair.

grounding: A child resents being told to share because a brother is younger, then explains which items can be lent.

passage: Thomas heard the crack when the pen hit the tiles and knew at once it was broken. It was Chandni's favourite gel pen, the blue one with a silver clip. That evening his elder sister searched the whole room, upset. "Did anyone take my pen?" Thomas kept his eyes on his building blocks, his ears hot. "Maybe Mummy moved it," he said. Chandni's face fell, and that hurt more than a scolding would have. At bedtime he crept to her desk and put the broken pen down. "I broke it. I'm sorry. I'll use my pocket money to get you a new one." She looked at it for a while, sighed, and said, "Thanks for telling me."

qa.q: What colour was Chandni's favourite pen?
qa.a: It was blue with a silver clip.

qa.q: Why did Thomas say "Maybe Mummy moved it"?
qa.a: He was afraid of trouble and hid that he broke the pen, but his hot ears show he felt uneasy about the lie.

qa.q: What did Thomas do at bedtime that repaired things better than lying?
qa.a: He admitted he broke it, apologised and offered to replace it with his pocket money.

qa.q: How might Chandni see the earlier lie compared with the later admission?
qa.a: Chandni's face fell at the lie, so she likely felt let down, but the truth and the apology let her sigh and thank him.

grounding: A child hides that he broke his sister's pen, then confesses, apologises and offers to replace it.

passage: I'm Rekha. For weeks I was sure Mummy and Papa loved my little sister Charu more. They came to her school events, cut her fruit, sat by her bed when she had a cold, and to me they said, "You're big now, you can manage." I began leaving my plate unwashed and answering back, thinking that if I was the trouble one, they might look at me. One evening Papa asked, "Rekha, what is going on?" and I burst out, "You never have time for me." He was quiet, then said Charu needed extra help with reading right now, which did not make me matter less. We planned a Saturday walk just for the two of us.

qa.q: What did Papa and Rekha plan for Saturday?
qa.a: They planned a Saturday walk just for the two of them.

qa.q: Why did Rekha start answering back and leaving plates unwashed?
qa.a: Rekha felt the parents loved Charu more and hoped that being the trouble one would make them notice.

qa.q: What did Rekha do that helped more than acting out?
qa.a: Rekha told Papa honestly, "You never have time for me," which led to a regular walk for the two of them.

qa.q: How might Papa see the difference between Rekha's and Charu's needs?
qa.a: Papa sees that Charu needs extra help with reading right now, which does not mean Rekha is loved less.

grounding: A child feels a sibling is favoured, acts out, then tells the father and gets one-to-one time.

passage: Friday: Hemant and Omkar fought over the last mango slice, and Omkar called his big brother Hemant stupid. A cushion flew across the room. Saturday: They argued about the remote, about whose shoe was on whose side, and Hemant shouted, "You are the worst brother ever!" Omkar cried a little and stormed out. Sunday: The power went off in the rain. They dragged bedsheets and chairs into the middle of the room and built a fort by torchlight. "Sorry I said worst," Hemant muttered. "Sorry I said stupid," said Omkar. They lay inside whispering jokes until Mummy peeked in, smiled and switched off the fan.

qa.q: What did the brothers build on Sunday night?
qa.a: They built a fort out of bedsheets and chairs.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when he muttered his apology in the fort?
qa.a: He probably felt regret about the hurtful thing he said and wanted to make up, since he apologised first. 🙂

qa.q: What helped the brothers repair after two days of fighting?
qa.a: They apologised for the specific insults and then did something fun together, building the fort.

qa.q: How might Omkar have felt when Hemant called him the worst brother ever?
qa.a: Omkar cried a little and stormed out, so the insult hurt him even though the brothers made up later.

grounding: Two siblings fight for days and then build a fort together, mixing irritation and love.

passage: Monday: Tejas teased his sister Diya about her missing front tooth until she squealed. Wednesday: At the park, Hrithik from the next lane shoved Diya off the swing, and she landed on her hands. Tejas dropped his bat and ran. He stood in front of her and said, "Don't touch my sister." His voice shook, but his fists stayed open. He took Diya's hand, walked her home and told Papa what happened. Friday: Tejas was calling Diya "gap-tooth" again, but he gave her the bigger half of his biscuit while he did it.

qa.q: Who shoved Diya off the swing?
qa.a: Hrithik from the next lane shoved her off the swing.

qa.q: Why did Tejas stand in front of Diya even though he teases her himself?
qa.a: He may tease her, but she is his sister, and he felt protective when someone else hurt her.

qa.q: What did Tejas do after defending Diya that kept things from turning violent?
qa.a: He took her hand, walked her home and told Papa instead of hitting Hrithik.

qa.q: How might Diya see Tejas after the swing incident?
qa.a: Diya probably feels safe and cared for because her brother stood up for her, even though he still teases her a little.

grounding: A sibling who teases his sister still defends her from an outsider, then tells a parent without violence.

passage: Omkar, you look just like I did at ten. Let me tell you about the vase. My brother Ravi and I were wrestling when something crashed. Amma came running and shouted at me alone, because I was the elder boy. "It was Ravi's elbow!" I wanted to say, but my voice stuck in my throat. I stood there burning, and later I kicked Ravi's slippers under the bed. That night Amma sat beside me and asked, "What really happened?" She listened all the way through. I noticed that anyone who feels unheard just gets angrier, and at the wrong person. So when my grandchildren quarrel, I ask each child first. -- Hemant

qa.q: What were Hemant and Ravi doing when something crashed?
qa.a: They were wrestling.

qa.q: What did Hemant want to say when Amma shouted at him, and why could he not?
qa.a: He wanted to say it was Ravi's elbow, but his voice stuck in his throat because he was burning with the unfairness.

qa.q: What did Amma do later that made things better?
qa.a: She sat beside Hemant, asked what really happened and listened all the way through.

qa.q: What would change if Amma had asked both boys before scolding?
qa.a: Hemant would not have felt the burning unfairness or taken it out on Ravi's slippers, and both boys could have told their side.

grounding: An elder recalls being scolded unheard as a boy and how being asked later eased it.

passage: I'm Kashish. For about a month I ran to Mummy every time Sachin did anything. "Mummy, he looked at me!" "Mummy, he took my eraser!" I wanted him to get punished. One evening Mummy sighed and said, "Kashish, I can't tell which times matter." That stung. I thought about it while brushing my teeth. The next day Sachin used my sharpener, and I said, "Please ask first." He said okay, and that was that. Then he hid my shoe near the stairs, which was dangerous, and that time I did tell Mummy. She came at once. I am learning to tell the difference.

qa.q: What did Kashish say to Sachin when he used the sharpener?
qa.a: Kashish said, "Please ask first."

qa.q: Why did Kashish run to Mummy about every small thing?
qa.a: Kashish wanted Sachin to get punished.

qa.q: How can Kashish decide when to tell Mummy and when to handle it alone?
qa.a: Kashish can handle small things by speaking to Sachin and tell Mummy when someone could really get hurt, as with the hidden shoe near the stairs.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel about hearing so many small complaints?
qa.a: Mummy sighed and said she could not tell which times mattered, so she probably found it hard to know when to step in.

grounding: A child who tattles constantly learns to handle small issues alone and tell adults about real harm.

passage: Sunday. Dhruvi followed me from my room to the balcony and all the way to the bathroom door. Then she touched my eraser collection and lined the erasers up wrong. I snapped, "Stop it, they're mine!" and her lip wobbled. She said, "I just want to be like you, Bhaiya." I felt bad, because it is annoying but also kind of sweet. So I made a plan. I told her the collection is mine and she can look but must ask before touching, and every day at five we will play a game together. She said okay and smiled 😊. Tomorrow I will see if it works. -- Yogesh

qa.q: What did Dhruvi touch and line up wrong?
qa.a: She touched Yogesh's eraser collection and lined the erasers up wrong.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh feel bad after snapping at Dhruvi?
qa.a: Her lip wobbled and she said she just wanted to be like him, so he realised she looks up to him.

qa.q: What kind limit did Yogesh set with Dhruvi?
qa.a: He told her the collection is his and she must ask before touching, and promised a game together every day at five.

qa.q: How might Dhruvi feel about Yogesh's rule?
qa.a: She said okay and smiled, so she may be a little disappointed about the erasers but glad to have a regular time with her big brother.

grounding: An older sibling who is irritated by a clingy younger sister sets a kind limit and offers shared time.
